entries.label: Labour productivity gain per unit cut in occupational entry regulation stringency
entries.units: % of labour productivity per unit of the OECD occupational entry regulation indicator (0–6)

citation.authors: Indre Bambalaite, Giuseppe Nicoletti and Christina von Rueden
citation.title: Occupational entry regulations and their effects on productivity in services: Firm-level evidence
citation.publisher: OECD Economics Department Working Papers No. 1605, ECO/WKP(2020)13
citation.locator: para. 44, p. 23 (PDF p. 24); Table 3, column II, row 'Indicator', p. 25 (PDF p. 26)
citation.version: Copy read from bollettinoadapt.it (53 pp.); the DOI is the official landing page

entries.quote: A one unit reduction in the full indicator (which would correspond to a significant reform, given that the average level of the indicator is 0.7) is associated with an increase in labour productivity by 1.6 percentage points of the average firm
entries.derivation: Value = the paper's 1.6 (Table 3 column II coefficient −0.0166, s.e. 0.00823). Range = its 95% interval: 1.66 ± 1.96 × 0.823, i.e. 0.05 to 3.27.
entries.notes: This is the elasticity the PC used (PC 2024, Box B3.4, p. 131: "a 1 unit decrease in their stringency indicator increased labour productivity by 1.6% (2020, p. 23)"). The paper's dependent variable is labour productivity growth of the average firm; the PC, and this tool, apply it as a one-off level effect (A-P14). The PC also assumed a 0.5-unit cut (entry c8.pc-stringency-cut.pc2024). Cross-country firm-level correlation, graded C as in the plan.

entries.label: Cut in stringency the PC assumed for its licensing simulation (L2), for reproducing it
entries.units: index points of the occupational entry regulation indicator

citation.title: National Competition Policy: modelling proposed reforms (study report with appendices)
citation.locator: Appendix B3, L2, p. 131 (PDF p. 137); Table C.7, p. 224 (PDF p. 230)

entries.quote: To reflect this, a 0.5 unit reduction in stringency was assumed, which translates to a 0.8% increase in labour productivity. … Modelled shock: Labour productivity is 0.8% higher in the 15 industries affected.
entries.derivation: Value = the PC's assumed cut (0.5 units). Fixed: used only to rebuild the PC's L2 shock (0.5 × 1.6% = 0.8%); a brief sets its own stringency change.
entries.notes: The PC chose a half-unit cut because it applied the shock to whole industries, which contain many unlicensed occupations. The tool weights by the employment share of the licensed occupations instead (A-P08), so this value is for the back-test and the PC chain reproduction (plan §8). PC sensitivity: 100%, 75%, 50% and 25% shocks give GDP +$10,333m, $7,750m, $5,167m and $2,583m (Table B3.4, p. 134).

entries.label: Share of the non-compete wage effect taken as a labour productivity gain

citation.title: National Competition Policy: modelling proposed reforms (study report with appendices)
citation.locator: Appendix B3, L1, p. 122 (PDF p. 128); lower bound, p. 127 (PDF p. 133)

entries.quote: As a result, 10% of the wage uplift estimated in Johnson, Lavetti and Lipsitz was applied as an increase in labour productivity. The increase of 10% was chosen to measure the elasticity of any change to economic output in response to any policy change. … The lower bound of sensitivity testing for the reform (a shock of size 50%) suggests that real GDP would increase by 0.1% (about $2.57 billion)
entries.derivation: Value = the PC's central assumption (10%); low = its lower-bound case, a shock half the size (5%); high = value, because the PC's central case is the top of its range.
entries.notes: An arbitrary assumption by the PC ("chosen to measure the elasticity"), graded C as in the plan. The Government's "$5 billion or 0.2 per cent to GDP" is this upper case (plan §3.2). With e61's 4% wage gap instead of JLL, the PC's GDP gain was 105% larger (p. 127). The wage effects themselves are fixed (entries c8.wage-*), so the PC's range is carried here only once (A-P15).

entries.label: Wage effect of lower non-compete enforceability, industries that use non-competes heavily
entries.units: % of earnings (25th to 75th percentile of US enforceability)

citation.title: National Competition Policy: modelling proposed reforms (study report with appendices)

entries.quote: ‘high’ clause use industries were assumed to receive a larger increase in labour productivity, as per the 2.4% increase in wages estimated in the study. After applying the 10% assumption, this resulted in a 0.24% increase in labour productivity
entries.derivation: Value = the PC's figure from Johnson, Lavetti and Lipsitz (2.4%). Fixed: the PC's range is carried by passThrough (A-P15).
entries.notes: Checked against the primary source: Johnson, Lavetti and Lipsitz, NBER Working Paper 31929 (revised December 2024), p. 22 (PDF p. 24): "Going from the 25th to 75th percentile of enforceability leads to a 2.4% decrease in earnings in high-use industries (p < 0.01)". A difference-in-differences design on US state law changes. The PC applied 0.24% in 24 service industries (Table C.7, p. 224).

entries.label: Wage effect of lower non-compete enforceability, other industries
entries.units: % of earnings (25th to 75th percentile of US enforceability)

citation.title: National Competition Policy: modelling proposed reforms (study report with appendices)

entries.quote: ‘low’ clause use industries were assumed to receive a slightly smaller increase in labour productivity, as per the 1.4% increase in wages estimated in the study. After applying the 10% assumption, this resulted in a 0.14% increase in labour productivity.
entries.derivation: Value = the PC's figure from Johnson, Lavetti and Lipsitz (1.4%). Fixed (A-P15).
entries.notes: The PC cites the 2023 version of the paper (p. 26). The revised December 2024 version (p. 22) says only that the effect for low-use industries "is roughly 60% as large" as 2.4% (about 1.44%); the 1.4% figure itself was not found in the version read. The PC applied 0.14% to all other industries except agriculture (Table C.7, p. 224).

entries.label: Share of Australian workers bound by a non-compete clause (the baseline a coverage change is scaled against)

citation.title: National Competition Policy: modelling proposed reforms (study report with appendices)

entries.quote: One in five Australian workers are subject to non-compete clauses and one in two are subject to some form of post-employment restraint (ABS 2024g).
entries.derivation: Value = one in five = 0.2. Fixed: a measured share; the uncertainty of the non-compete effect is carried by the pass-through and wage-effect entries.
entries.notes: Used to scale a brief's change in coverage against a full ban (interpretation A-P09): a ban is a change of −0.2, which gives the PC's L1 shock. The PC modelled L1 as a ban on unreasonable restraints, so a partial change is a linear share of it (the PC found its results roughly linear in the shock).
